paragraphs: A synthetic data generator can produce convincing examples without providing an explicit formula for their probabilities. This creates a problem for statistical checks that depend on knowing that formula. The paper develops a goodness-of-fit procedure for assessing whether an implicit generator matches the observed data it is intended to reproduce.

The method builds a test related to Kernelised Stein Discrepancy. Its central component is a nonparametric Stein operator estimated using samples drawn from the generator. In practical terms, the assessment machinery is learned from generated examples, allowing the procedure to work without an explicit probability distribution. The approach also distinguishes two sources of evidence: the observed dataset has a fixed size, while additional synthetic samples can be requested from the model.

Experiments cover synthetic distributions and trained generators using both synthetic and real datasets. The reported improvement is in statistical power: the test is better able to identify mismatches in those comparisons. This supports its usefulness as a generator assessment method, rather than establishing that any particular generator produces adequate data.
neurips-2022-a-kernelised-stein-statisti.tldr: A sample-based Stein test assesses implicit data generators and shows improved power to detect distributional mismatches in experiments.

paragraphs: Survival analysis often involves censored data, where the target outcome is only partially observed. This paper uses neural networks to predict quantiles of that outcome directly. A collection of quantiles describes different positions in the predicted outcome distribution, providing uncertainty information without requiring a particular distributional form.

The authors first adapt an algorithm used with linear models to neural networks. That adaptation requires training a separate network for each requested quantile in sequence, making the procedure inefficient. Their main contribution replaces this sequence with one network that outputs a grid of quantiles and an algorithm that optimizes those outputs together. This combines flexible prediction with a more unified treatment of the requested uncertainty estimates.

The paper provides two theoretical perspectives on the algorithm: an interpretation through expectation-maximisation and a self-correcting property. Experimentally, its predicted quantiles are better calibrated than existing methods on 10 of 12 real datasets. Better calibration means the quantile predictions more closely match their intended probability levels, supporting the method's usefulness for uncertainty estimation on those datasets.
neurips-2022-censored-quantile-regressio.tldr: One neural network jointly learns censored outcome quantiles, improving calibration over existing methods on 10 of 12 real datasets.

paragraphs: Predicting future human motion within a 3D scene requires more than extending a sequence of body poses. The body's movement must remain consistent with its surroundings. The paper identifies implicit treatment of human-scene interactions as a source of artifacts, including ghost motion, when local body configurations and overall movement are insufficiently constrained.

The proposed method makes contact relationships explicit through distance-based maps connecting every body joint to every scene point at each time. It uses a two-stage pipeline: first predict future contact maps from previous maps and the scene point cloud, then predict future poses conditioned on those contact forecasts. Contacts therefore become an intermediate prediction that directly guides how the body moves through the environment.

During training, a prior built from contact maps and future poses encourages agreement between local poses and global movement. The method outperforms the compared motion forecasting and human synthesis approaches on synthetic and real datasets. These findings support explicit contact modeling as a useful way to improve scene-aware forecasts, without implying that every predicted interaction is physically correct.
neurips-2022-contact-aware-human-motion-.tldr: Predicting human-scene contacts before body poses improves scene-aware motion forecasting on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Chebyshev polynomials have strong approximation properties, yet graph neural networks using them have sometimes performed worse than simpler or alternative polynomial constructions. This paper investigates that apparent contradiction in ChebNet, which approximates spectral graph convolutions using a Chebyshev basis. The question is whether the basis itself explains the disappointing results.

The authors attribute ChebNet's weaker performance primarily to learned coefficients that are unsuitable for approximating analytic filter functions, leading to overfitting. They introduce ChebNetII, which uses Chebyshev interpolation to improve the approximation. The design also reduces the Runge phenomenon, an unwanted oscillatory behavior associated with polynomial approximation. This shifts attention from the choice of polynomial family to how its coefficients and resulting filters are constructed.

Experiments show that ChebNetII can learn arbitrary graph convolutions and achieves superior performance in the evaluated fully supervised and semi-supervised node classification tasks. The authors also scale it to ogbn-papers100M. Together, these results support revisiting spectral graph networks with improved approximation design, rather than treating earlier ChebNet results as evidence against the Chebyshev basis.
neurips-2022-convolutional-neural-networ.tldr: ChebNetII improves spectral graph learning through Chebyshev interpolation, addressing coefficient-related overfitting in the original ChebNet.

paragraphs: Online learning processes examples sequentially, and computational efficiency can prevent an algorithm from achieving the best statistically possible regret. This paper studies a smoothed setting: Nature may choose incoming contexts, but their density relative to a known reference measure is bounded by 1/σ. That restriction is part of the setting supporting the results.

For realizable K-wise linear classification, the authors give a computationally efficient algorithm attaining the statistically optimal log(T/σ) regret dependence. Realizability means the setting assumes a true classifier within the relevant class. The results also extend to classifiers linear in an over-parameterized polynomial feature representation, and to realizable piecewise regression when an appropriate empirical risk minimization oracle is available.

The analysis requires more than standard arguments based on regions where candidate classifiers disagree. The authors develop a new geometric characterization of those regions for generalized linear classifiers, along with technical tools including a determinant anti-concentration bound. The contribution connects computational efficiency with optimal statistical behavior under the stated smoothing and realizability conditions.
neurips-2022-efficient-and-near-optimal-.tldr: Under smoothing and realizability assumptions, an efficient online classification algorithm attains statistically optimal logarithmic regret.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve resistance to adversarial examples while harming standard visual task performance. The authors contrast this with benefits observed in language tasks and suggest that discrete, symbolic inputs could help explain the difference. Their method, Discrete Adversarial Training, brings that input structure into visual learning.

DAT uses VQGAN to convert images into discrete visual words. Training then minimizes worst-case risk under symbolic perturbations to these discrete images. The intervention therefore changes the space in which adversarial examples are constructed. The paper also offers a distribution-based explanation for why this procedure can improve visual representations, and presents DAT as a component that can be added to existing training approaches.

Experiments report improvements in image classification, object detection, and self-supervised learning. A model pretrained with Masked Auto-Encoding and then fine-tuned using DAT, without additional data, achieves 31.40 mCE on ImageNet-C and 32.77% top-1 accuracy on Stylized-ImageNet, reported as state of the art. These findings support discrete adversarial perturbations as a useful training choice in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-enhance-the-visual-represen.tldr: Discrete Adversarial Training perturbs visual words and improves performance across several visual learning tasks.

paragraphs: A distance oracle preprocesses a dataset so that distances from a new query to all stored points can be approximated quickly. Directly processing every coordinate of every point takes roughly nd work for n points in d dimensions. The paper extends efficient distance-oracle constructions from familiar norm families to any symmetric norm.

The proposed data structure returns approximations within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± ε. Its scope includes ℓp and Orlicz norms, as well as top-k norms, mixtures of ℓp norms, small-support norms, and the box-norm. This matters because the distance definition can vary across applications, while the construction provides a common approach across this broader class.

Preprocessing time and storage are approximately n(d + mmc(l)²), and query time is approximately d + n·mmc(l)², with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here mmc(l) measures the complexity of the chosen symmetric norm. The efficiency therefore depends on that norm-specific quantity. For ℓp norms, the runtime matches the previously established state-of-the-art oracles, extending coverage while retaining their known efficiency in that case.
neurips-2022-fast-distance-oracles-for-a.tldr: A distance-oracle construction supports every symmetric norm, with efficiency governed by a norm-specific complexity measure.

paragraphs: Matching an image with a caption does not directly identify which visual region corresponds to each phrase. Many vision-language methods learn from whole-image and whole-text alignment, leaving these finer semantic relationships implicit. LOUPE addresses the challenge of learning region-to-phrase alignment when training information is available only at the image-text pair level.

The framework approaches fine-grained alignment through game-theoretic interactions. It introduces an uncertainty-aware neural module for learning Shapley interactions efficiently, making those interaction estimates part of the alignment approach. The central idea is to extract more detailed semantic structure from the relationships within paired visual and textual information, rather than requiring object-level human annotations to supply that structure.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across a variety of vision-language tasks. LOUPE also achieves competitive object detection and visual grounding performance without object-level human annotations or fine-tuning. These findings suggest that raw image-text pairs can provide useful supervision for localized semantic understanding, beyond learning whether an entire image and caption belong together.
neurips-2022-fine-grained-semantically-a.tldr: LOUPE uses game-theoretic interactions to learn region-to-phrase alignment from image-text pairs without object-level annotations.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a human's 3D shape from a single view requires a representation that supports both detailed geometry and fast computation. The paper introduces Fourier Occupancy Field, or FOF, to address the difficulty of obtaining high-quality reconstruction at real-time speed with existing representations.

FOF organizes geometry on a 2D field perpendicular to the viewing direction. At each location, a short Fourier series describes occupancy along the corresponding depth direction. Those coefficients can be stored as channels of an image, making the representation compatible with 2D convolutional networks while preserving topology and neighborhood relationships in the 2D domain. This provides a direct connection between image-based processing and the representation of 3D shape.

The representation supports conversion to and from meshes, and can incorporate parametric models as priors for more robust results. Using FOF, the authors build a high-fidelity monocular human reconstruction framework operating above 30 frames per second. Demonstrations on public datasets and captured real data support the representation's potential to combine reconstruction quality, speed, and flexibility.
neurips-2022-fof-learning-fourier-occupa.tldr: FOF encodes depth occupancy as image-like Fourier coefficients, enabling high-fidelity monocular human reconstruction above 30 frames per second.

paragraphs: An agent following human commands may need to obey an instruction even when it reduces the chance of winning. This paper defines Grounded Reinforcement Learning around that combination: accomplishing a demanding task while following high-level language commands. Success therefore involves both task performance and responsiveness to human direction.

The authors explain why either ordinary reinforcement learning or behavior cloning alone is inadequate for this problem. Abstract commands can permit many complicated behaviors, making precise reward design difficult. Demonstrations also reflect human strategies that may be suboptimal. The proposed approach uses a constrained reinforcement learning objective and an iterative algorithm called REinforced demonstration Distillation, or RED, to learn a policy for this combined goal.

Evaluation uses the simplified real-time strategy game MiniRTS, comparing RED with behavior cloning and pure reinforcement learning. Experiments and human studies find that RED consistently follows commands while achieving a higher win rate than those baselines. The results demonstrate the approach's value in that game setting, where command adherence and competitive performance must be handled together.
neurips-2022-grounded-reinforcement-lear.tldr: RED combines constrained reinforcement learning with demonstration distillation to follow human commands and improve win rates in MiniRTS.

paragraphs: HALO is a generative model designed to separate what an image sequence contains from how that information changes over time. Content captures summary information about the sequence, while motion controls its dynamic expression. Separating these factors makes it possible to change motion while retaining another sequence's content.

The model represents latent dynamics using Hamiltonian motion. This gives the motion a reversible structure and a volume-preserving organization in phase space. The authors use that structure to obtain continuous, nondivergent latent paths and to connect similarity between frames with proximity of their phase-space coordinates. These properties are intended to support both disentanglement and generation over longer sequences.

To distinguish different kinds of dynamics over time, HALO assigns each motion its own Hamiltonian acting within a corresponding subspace. This organization supports controlled generation by keeping motion types separately represented. The paper demonstrates the model through motion swapping between sequence pairs, controlled generation, and image rotation tasks. These demonstrations show how structured latent dynamics can provide usable controls over generated sequences.
neurips-2022-hamiltonian-latent-operator.tldr: HALO uses Hamiltonian latent dynamics to separate sequence content from motion and enable controlled generation.

paragraphs: Event clouds have an irregular, sparse structure with high temporal resolution. Converting them into conventional images makes established tracking methods easier to use, but compromises those characteristics. This paper develops an end-to-end tracker that processes event clouds directly, with components designed around their unusual spatial and temporal organization.

A density-insensitive downsampling strategy selects a subset of key events from the large, unevenly distributed cloud. A graph network embeds their spatial and temporal information. One branch estimates how likely each event belongs to the target through semantic Siamese matching. Another learns motion flow, traces potential earlier event positions backward, and compares them with the previous target proposal.

Each branch uses its target likelihoods to weight event embeddings and predict a bounding box. The tracker then adaptively combines the two boxes, bringing together semantic matching and motion-based evidence. Experiments on synthetic and real event datasets report better tracking accuracy and speed than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The results support tailoring the tracking pipeline to event data rather than first reorganizing it into frames.
neurips-2022-learning-graph-embedded-key.tldr: A graph-based tracker processes event clouds directly and combines semantic matching with motion back-tracing to improve accuracy and speed.

paragraphs: Domain decomposition solves a partial differential equation by working with smaller subdomains. How those pieces communicate at their interfaces is crucial to constructing an effective solver. Optimizing that communication traditionally requires substantial analysis, and available constructions often depend on simplified settings with structured grids.

The paper extends optimized Schwarz domain decomposition to unstructured grids using graph convolutional neural networks. Through unsupervised learning, the networks learn modifications at subdomain interfaces. This places learning at the point where separate local calculations must interact, while retaining the domain decomposition approach to solving the overall equation.

An improved loss function is central to the method. The authors report that it enables training on relatively small problems while supporting robust performance on arbitrarily large ones, with computational cost linear in problem size. They compare the resulting linear solvers with classical and optimized domain decomposition algorithms on structured and unstructured grids. The contribution is a route to learning interface behavior that transfers across problem scales and extends solver construction beyond the structured settings where analytic optimization is more readily available.
neurips-2022-learning-interface-conditio.tldr: Graph networks learn domain decomposition interface conditions on small problems, supporting scalable solvers on unstructured grids.

paragraphs: Numerical PDE solvers use meshes to divide a physical domain into manageable pieces. Moving mesh points can improve accuracy by concentrating resolution where the solution needs it and reducing unnecessary resolution elsewhere. Sophisticated movement methods can nevertheless be expensive because they require solving additional equations each time the mesh adapts.

M2N introduces an end-to-end learned approach to mesh movement. Its designs address mesh tangling, consistency at domain boundaries, and transfer across mesh resolutions. A neural spline model offers flexibility for large deformations, while a graph attention model handles more complicated domain shapes and finer local changes. These alternatives target different demands within the same mesh adaptation problem.

The authors evaluate stationary and time-dependent equations, linear and nonlinear equations, and domains with regular and irregular shapes. Compared with the traditional Monge-Ampère approach, their methods accelerate mesh adaptation by three to four orders of magnitude while achieving comparable reductions in numerical error. The reported speedup concerns adaptation itself, showing how learning can reduce the overhead of repeatedly repositioning a solver's mesh.
neurips-2022-m2n-mesh-movement-networks-.tldr: M2N learns to move PDE solver meshes, accelerating adaptation by three to four orders of magnitude with comparable error reduction.

paragraphs: Continual learning systems can forget earlier tasks as they learn new ones. Experience replay addresses this by retaining a small collection of past examples for reuse. This paper focuses on how that memory is constructed, treating the choice of stored examples as an active optimization problem rather than a fixed policy.

The authors formulate dynamic memory construction as combinatorial optimization aimed at reducing loss across all tasks encountered so far. They first explore three tactics in an offline setting. For online continual learning, they introduce Global Pseudo-task Simulation, or GPS, as an approximate solution. GPS uses permutations to simulate how the current task might later be forgotten, providing information to guide memory construction.

Empirical results and analyses suggest that GPS consistently improves accuracy across four commonly used vision benchmarks. The authors also show that existing memory construction policies can be integrated within its framework. This makes the contribution both a particular simulation-based strategy and a way to organize replay memory choices around performance across experienced tasks.
neurips-2022-navigating-memory-construct.tldr: GPS simulates future forgetting to guide replay memory construction and improves accuracy across four continual learning vision benchmarks.

paragraphs: Hierarchical variational autoencoders can capture higher-level semantic information useful for identifying inputs outside a model's training distribution. The paper finds that posterior collapse can seriously restrict this ability. In this context, the problem is that latent representations fail to retain enough useful connection to individual data samples.

The authors propose an informative hierarchical VAE that strengthens connections between each input and its stochastic latent representations across multiple layers during training. This aims to alleviate posterior collapse, making the hierarchy a more useful source of information for detection. The architecture change addresses the quality of the representations before they are combined into a detection decision.

A second contribution, the Adaptive Likelihood Ratio, selectively aggregates semantic information from multiple hidden layers. The resulting score is designed to separate familiar samples from out-of-distribution ones. Experiments show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art unsupervised detection approaches. The findings support addressing both representation collapse and the way information from different levels is combined, rather than relying on hierarchical semantics alone.
neurips-2022-out-of-distribution-detecti.tldr: An informative hierarchical VAE and adaptive likelihood-ratio score improve unsupervised out-of-distribution detection in experiments.

paragraphs: High-dimensional estimation becomes difficult when observations include outliers and the desired answer must satisfy sparsity constraints. This paper studies two central examples: estimating a sparse mean and performing sparse principal component analysis robustly. It asks how these statistical goals can be expressed as optimization problems that are practical to solve.

The authors construct simple nonconvex formulations with a strong connection between optimization progress and statistical quality. For these formulations, any approximate stationary point yields a near-optimal solution to the corresponding robust estimation problem. Stationarity is therefore sufficient for the stated statistical result; an optimization method does not need to establish that it has found a global optimum.

A consequence is that any first-order method that efficiently reaches stationarity provides an efficient algorithm for these estimation tasks. That qualification matters: the result transfers efficiency from a suitable optimization method rather than asserting it for every possible procedure. The resulting algorithms are described as practical and successful under broader distributional assumptions than previous work, connecting robust sparse statistics with accessible nonconvex optimization.
neurips-2022-outlier-robust-sparse-estim.tldr: New nonconvex formulations make approximate stationarity sufficient for near-optimal robust sparse mean estimation and sparse PCA.

paragraphs: In a flow network, supplies and demands are specified at nodes, while the quantities of interest move along edges. This paper estimates edge flows that lack labels from the available nodal information. It builds physical relationships directly into a neural network layer so that prediction reflects the structure of the flow problem.

The implicit layer combines conservation of mass with a constitutive relationship linking edge flows to nodal states, such as Ohm's law. Together, these laws define a nonlinear inverse problem. A specialized contraction mapping efficiently solves that problem to obtain the flows. The layer's output is thus determined through solving the physical relationships rather than through an unconstrained direct prediction.

Implicit differentiation provides gradients through the solution, allowing the constitutive relationship itself to be learned in a semi-supervised framework. This combines known conservation structure with a relationship inferred from data. Experiments on AC power networks and water distribution systems demonstrate accurate edge-flow predictions, supporting the approach across the two types of network considered.
neurips-2022-physics-informed-implicit-r.tldr: An implicit neural layer combines flow conservation with a learned constitutive relationship to predict unlabeled network edge flows.

paragraphs: This paper studies control of an unknown linear dynamical system when the cost of actions can change adversarially over time. The controller receives full feedback about both the system state and the cost function. Its performance is measured against the best stabilizing linear controller that could have been chosen with hindsight.

The authors present a computationally efficient algorithm with an optimal regret rate proportional to the square root of the time horizon T. Regret measures the accumulated performance gap relative to that hindsight comparator. The guarantee allows convex costs without requiring stronger conditions such as strong convexity, broadening the cost functions covered by this efficient control result.

The method carefully constructs lower confidence bounds for the online costs. Although these bounds are nonconvex, their particular structure allows a new efficient regret-minimization technique. The main contribution combines a favorable statistical rate with computational tractability under unknown dynamics. Its scope remains the stated setting of linear systems, convex changing costs, full feedback, and comparison with stabilizing linear controllers.
neurips-2022-rate-optimal-online-convex-.tldr: An efficient adaptive controller achieves optimal square-root regret for unknown linear systems with adversarial convex costs and full feedback.

paragraphs: Some problems have simple, efficient learning algorithms but remain difficult for neural networks to learn efficiently. The paper asks whether a network can discover such algorithms itself. It provides a theoretical architecture that learns in polynomial time as well as any efficient learning algorithm expressible by a constant-sized program.

The construction combines recurrent weight sharing across layers with convolutional weight sharing. Together, these mechanisms keep the number of parameters constant even when the network has an enormous number of nodes. Parity learning illustrates the result: the network can learn as well as Gaussian elimination, an efficient algorithm with a concise description.

The distinction between parameter count and overall computational scale is central to interpreting the finding. The architecture can contain trillions of nodes, and the authors explicitly state that the constants in their analysis are too large for direct practical significance. The result instead suggests a theoretical advantage of combining recurrence and convolution when representing discrete learning algorithms concisely; it does not establish a ready-to-use practical learner.
neurips-2022-recurrent-convolutional-neu.tldr: A theoretical recurrent-convolutional architecture can match succinct efficient learning algorithms, although its constants make the construction impractical.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image location, making inference speed important when predictions must arrive in real time. Transformers have achieved strong segmentation results, but their computation can be costly. RTFormer redesigns transformer components to improve the balance between segmentation performance and efficiency on GPU-like devices.

The model uses two resolutions and a GPU-friendly attention mechanism with linear complexity. It also removes the multi-head mechanism. Cross-resolution attention transfers high-level information from the low-resolution branch to the high-resolution branch. This lets the finer representation receive global context through information already learned at a coarser resolution, which the authors find more efficient for gathering that context.

Experiments show a better performance-efficiency tradeoff than CNN-based models in the evaluated comparisons. RTFormer reports state-of-the-art results on Cityscapes, CamVid, and COCOStuff, with promising results on ADE20K. The contribution is an architecture whose attention and information exchange are designed around efficient inference, showing that transformers can be competitive for real-time segmentation when those computational choices are addressed directly.
neurips-2022-rtformer-efficient-design-f.tldr: RTFormer combines efficient attention and cross-resolution context sharing to improve the speed-accuracy tradeoff in real-time semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Spectral bias is the tendency of neural networks to learn lower-frequency functions preferentially. It has been proposed as one explanation for their generalization, but much evidence came from simplified settings. This paper develops ways to measure the phenomenon in modern image classifiers on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet.

The measurements reveal spectral bias, but the relationship with accuracy is more nuanced than a preference for uniformly smoother functions. On CIFAR-10, interventions that improve test accuracy tend to produce higher function frequencies overall and lower frequencies near examples within each class. This pattern appears across changes in training duration, architecture, dataset size, augmentation, and self-distillation.

The authors also distinguish learned function frequency from frequency within the input images. They find sensitivity to the low image frequencies common in natural images. On ImageNet, more internally diverse classes correspond to higher learned function frequencies. These findings provide measurement tools and empirical relationships that can inform explanations of generalization, while stopping short of establishing spectral bias as its complete or causal explanation.
neurips-2022-spectral-bias-in-practice-t.tldr: Measurements reveal spectral bias in practical image classifiers and link better accuracy to different frequency patterns globally and near same-class examples.

paragraphs: When one person's treatment affects someone else's outcome, standard independence assumptions for causal inference can fail. This paper targets the total treatment effect: the average outcome difference between treating the entire population and treating nobody. It asks how to estimate that quantity without knowing the network through which people influence one another.

The approach uses a staggered randomized rollout, gradually assigning treatment to random subsets of individuals. Observations from successive stages are connected to polynomial extrapolation, allowing the authors to construct unbiased estimators of the total treatment effect. The guarantee requires network interference to involve low-degree interactions among an individual's neighbors; it does not cover unrestricted forms of interference.

The authors derive variance bounds and compare their estimator with baselines on simulated data, where it performs well. The methodological value is that experimental rollout structure can support estimation even without prior structural knowledge of the network. The low-degree interaction condition remains essential to the stated unbiasedness result, while the experiments provide supporting evidence within simulated settings.
neurips-2022-staggered-rollout-designs-e.tldr: Staggered randomized rollouts enable unbiased total-effect estimation without network knowledge when interference has low-degree interactions.

paragraphs: Neural networks can serve as variational approximations to quantum states, offering an alternative for many-body problems where other numerical methods face difficulties. This paper studies how to systematically improve such representations. Its starting point is a construction that combines simple restricted Boltzmann machines rather than relying on one original variational family.

The proposed state is a symmetry-projected linear combination of these networks. Combining them allows the representation to reach states outside the original variational manifold, increasing expressive power with moderate computational effort. Symmetry projection also restores spatial symmetries. These components provide a structured way to enlarge the space of candidate quantum states.

The authors then use Lanczos recursion to build an expansion in Krylov states, which can further improve the approximation's accuracy. They demonstrate the approach on the square-lattice Heisenberg J1-J2 model and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for its ground-state representation. The result supports combining neural representations with symmetry and Lanczos-based refinement for this many-body problem; it does not establish a general resolution of the sign problem.
neurips-2022-systematic-improvement-of-n.tldr: Symmetry-projected combinations of neural quantum states and Lanczos refinement achieve state-of-the-art ground-state accuracy on the studied J1-J2 model.

paragraphs: Predicting how a small drug molecule binds to a protein requires understanding both the interaction geometry and the relevant protein region. The paper identifies weaknesses in earlier approaches, including limited conformation sampling and learned methods that neglect geometric constraints or underemphasize local functional regions. These weaknesses can produce unreasonable structures or poor generalization to unfamiliar proteins.

TANKBind builds trigonometric constraints into the neural model as an inductive bias, giving geometry an explicit role in prediction. It also divides the protein into functional blocks to attend to possible binding sites throughout the protein. This combines structural constraints with deliberate attention to local regions where binding may occur.

The training objective uses contrastive losses with negative examples sampled from local regions to jointly optimize binding interactions and affinity. Experiments report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art physics-based and deep learning methods on commonly used benchmarks, covering both binding structure and affinity prediction under varied settings. These results support the combined use of geometric structure and local binding-region information in the evaluated prediction tasks.
neurips-2022-tankbind-trigonometry-aware.tldr: TANKBind combines trigonometric constraints and local protein-region modeling to improve binding structure and affinity predictions on benchmarks.
